message:
MESSAGE:
ok so I'm trying to get my money life together lol. context: I'm 24, just started my first proper salaried job after two years of bar work, and for the first time ever I have a little bit of money that isn't already spoken for. a few things:

can you explain what an emergency fund is actually supposed to be for, like what counts as an emergency? and what's a good name for a savings pot in my banking app that'll actually stop me raiding it. also my friend keeps saying I should do a "no-spend month". give me three rules that would make one realistic and not miserable. and is a spreadsheet or an app better for tracking spending if I'm honestly kind of lazy? one-line answer is fine.

I've got $5,000 that I'm putting in a high-yield savings account at 4% a year, compounded monthly, and I'm leaving it completely alone for 3 years. I worked out I'll have $5,600 at the end (4% x 3 years = 12%, so $600 interest). is that right? what will it actually be?

last thing, rewrite this text to my landlord so it sounds less passive-aggressive: "As I have ALREADY mentioned twice, the bathroom fan is still broken." I don't want to start a war, I just want the fan fixed before winter.

thanks!! sorry this is so long, I've been putting all of this off for months and figured I'd just ask everything at once. my plan is to sit down sunday afternoon with a coffee and actually set all this up properly instead of just thinking about it, so whatever you send back is basically my to-do list for the weekend. (my parents are not money people at all, so I'm learning this from scratch and from tiktok, which is probably not ideal)

RESPONSE:
Great plan for Sunday. Here's everything, in order.

## 1. What an emergency fund is for

It's money for things that are **unexpected, necessary, and urgent**. If something doesn't meet all three, it isn't an emergency.

**Counts:**
- Losing your job or having your hours cut
- Medical or dental bills
- Urgent car repairs if you need the car for work
- An emergency flight home for a family crisis
- Essential things breaking, like your phone (if you need it for work) or your laptop

**Doesn't count:**
- Concert tickets, holidays, a sale
- Christmas and birthdays (they're predictable, so save for them separately)
- Annual bills you know are coming

**How much:** Start with a first goal of **$1,000**, then build to **3–6 months of essential expenses** (rent, bills, food, transport). Coming from bar work, the 3-month target alone will feel like a big win.

## 2. A name for the savings pot

Make the name a question you have to answer before you take money out:

- **"Is this actually an emergency?"** ← my top pick
- "Future Me Is Begging You"
- "Do Not Touch: Job Loss / Broken Car Only"

It also helps to keep this money at a **different bank** from your everyday account, so moving it takes a day and you get time to reconsider.

## 3. Three rules for a no-spend month that isn't miserable

1. **Essentials are always allowed.** Rent, bills, groceries, transport, medicine and toiletries are fine. The month only cuts the extras: takeaways, clothes, impulse buys, random Amazon orders.
2. **Give yourself one planned treat a week** with a set budget, like a $20 coffee-and-pastry fund or one dinner with friends. Having a planned outlet keeps you from quitting in week two.
3. **Use a 48-hour wishlist instead of banning things.** If you want something, write it down. If you still want it at the end of the month, you can buy it guilt-free. Most things won't survive the list.

Bonus: move whatever you didn't spend into your emergency fund on the last day so you can see what you saved.

## 4. Spreadsheet or app?

**Use an app.** If you're lazy, automatic tracking will beat a spreadsheet you stop updating by week three.

## 5. The savings maths

Your answer is close but a little low. **4% × 3 = 12%** is *simple* interest, which only pays interest on your original $5,000. With compounding, you also earn interest on the interest you've already earned.

**Monthly compounding:**
- Monthly rate = 4% ÷ 12 ≈ 0.333%
- Number of months = 3 × 12 = 36
- 5,000 × (1 + 0.04/12)³⁶ = 5,000 × 1.12727

**You'll have about $5,636.36**, which is about **$636 in interest**. That's roughly $36 more than your estimate, and you earn it without doing anything.

Two caveats:
- If the bank's "4%" is the **APY** (annual percentage yield, which usually includes compounding), you'd get 5,000 × 1.04³ ≈ **$5,624.32**. Check which one the account lists.
- Savings rates are usually **variable**, so the rate may change over 3 years. Interest is also usually taxable, so it's worth knowing that come tax time.

## 6. The text to your landlord

> Hi [Name], just following up on the bathroom fan, which still isn't working. I'd really like to get it sorted before winter so we don't end up with damp or mould issues. Could you let me know when someone might be able to come and take a look? Happy to work around their schedule. Thanks!

Mentioning damp and mould gives them a practical reason to act, since it protects their property, and it doesn't sound like a complaint. If this doesn't work, send the next message by email so you have a written record.

## Your Sunday to-do list

- [ ] Open a high-yield savings account and name the pot
- [ ] Set up an automatic transfer for payday, even a small one
- [ ] Download a spending-tracker app and link your accounts
- [ ] Decide when your no-spend month starts and write down your 3 rules
- [ ] Check whether your 4% rate is APR or APY
- [ ] Send the landlord text
- [ ] Enjoy the coffee ☕

Learning this from scratch at 24 puts you ahead of a lot of people.
